episodes.189077: A deep upper level trough was observed situated along the Mississippi River Valley during the morning of April 11th, with deep south-southwesterly windflow ahead of the trough carrying moisture from the Gulf of Mexico northward along the Appalachian chain.  Southeasterly windflow in the low levels of the atmosphere carried this moisture up the Blue Ridge escarpment, with the orographic lift enhancing rainfall totals across the headwaters of the Watauga River in Watauga and Avery Counties.  Rain began falling between 3:00 am and 4:00 am EDT across northwest North Carolina and persisted through the day, with rainfall rates varying 0.10 inch/hour and 0.70 inch/hour.  Rainfall totals for the day across the headwaters of the Watauga River ranged generally between 3.5 and 4.5 inches, with totals locally as high as 5 inches.
episodes.189108: A line of thunderstorms produced localized wind damage over portions of central Virginia into southern Maryland during the late evening to overnight hours.
episodes.189110: A line of thunderstorms produced localized wind damage over portions of central Virginia into southern Maryland during the late evening to overnight hours.
episodes.189119: A squall line ahead of a strong cold front produced a few gusts to storm force.
episodes.189127: A strong low pressure system to the northwest of the Hawaiian Islands along with an associated surface trough brought abundant moisture and an unstable atmosphere to the region. This moisture and instability led to heavy rainfall and thunderstorms primarily over the island of Kauai. During the early morning of April twelve, a band of heavy showers with embedded thunderstorms moved over the island of Kauai. There were several evacuations, road closures, and flooding reports that resulted over portions of Kauai.
episodes.189271: An unstable atmosphere and a strong upper level disturbance combined to bring several reports of tees down.
episodes.189432: A cold front brought widespread soaking rainfall to the area. This rainfall combined with significant snowpack loss and saturated grounds to produce minor to moderate river flooding, with isolated flash flooding across the mountains. Repeated rounds of rain compressed, warmed, and ripened the area snowpack in advance of the heavier rain on Friday the 12th.  The combination of rain, strong winds, and high dew points in excess of  50F over the ripe snow led to rapid melt with up to 4��� water loss. Complete melt-out occurred below 2,000 ft. The ground was bare south of the foothills; however soils were saturated and offered little storage for runoff. Rainfall ranged from 1 to 2 inches for most of the region, with amounts of 2 to 3 inches in the mountains.
episodes.189587: A low pressure over the Ohio Valley intensified as it lifted northeast. This potent frontal system brought a round of heavy rains, strong winds, and a few thunderstorms to southern New England Thursday night into Friday. This resulted in 1-2 inches of rain and some strong wind gusts but no damage or flooding.
episodes.189623: A potent system moved through the southern half of NC during the afternoon and evening hours, with thunderstorms becoming severe as they moved through the southern Piedmont of NC, and into the southern coastal plain counties, all the way to the coast through mid evening. Most of the severe reports were from thunderstorm winds, but isolated severe hail fell as well.
episodes.189708: Active weather in the form of strong thunderstorms occurred on the afternoon of April 11th, with main impacts observed in southwest Virginia occurring due to flash flooding. Heavy downpours associated with passing storms caused multiple road closures where high water issues occurred in Buchanan and Dickenson Counties. In Clinchco, local residents were stranded after their driveway was washed away. Shower and storm activity faded after sunset on the evening of April 11th, and the flooded roads gradually receded overnight into the morning of the 12th.
episodes.189709: Showers and thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of April 11th due to the combination of unseasonably warm temperatures and a passing disturbance. Storms crossed in from the Ohio River Valley during the early afternoon and continued an eastward progression into the evening. A swath of tree damage and power outages were observed from Mingo County to the eastern half of the West Virginia from damaging wind gusts. Storms pressed eastward late on the evening of April 11th.||In addition, numerous areas of flooding transpired that afternoon and evening in response to heavy downpours and training storms throughout the state. The Charleston airport set records for the wettest April as a result of observing 3.32 inches of rainfall on April 11th, breaking the old record of 1.83 inches set back in 1965.||High water issues along state roads were the main impacts from the flooding, some of which needed water rescues for cars that drove into these trouble spots. Excess water eventually drained into the Ohio River on the 12th and 13th of April, returning to its banks a few days later. One fatality occurred in Wood County on the 14th, when a motorist drove past high water signs and their vehicle became submerged.
episodes.189729: A strong mid-level trough and an associated frontal zone crossed through the|Mid-South and took aim on the OH Valley. Strong forcing associated the energy aloft coupled with a gradually destabilizing boundary layer out ahead it set the stage for areas of locally heavy showers and thunderstorms for several hours and prompted dangerous flash flooding. A flash flood emergency was issued for portions of Allegheny County when 4 to 5 inches of rain fell on the community of Oakdale, PA in less than 6 hours.  Elsewhere, flash flooding occurred along small tributaries with widespread rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches.
episodes.189730: A strong mid-level trough and an associated frontal zone crossed through the|Mid-South and took aim on the OH Valley. Strong forcing associated the energy aloft coupled with a gradually destabilizing boundary layer out ahead it set the stage for areas of locally heavy showers and thunderstorms for several hours and prompted dangerous flash flooding. A flash flood emergency was issued for portions of Allegheny County when 4 to 5 inches of rain fell on the community of Oakdale, PA in less than 6 hours.  Elsewhere, flash flooding occurred along small tributaries with widespread rainfall amounts of 2 to 3 inches.
episodes.189784: A strong area of low pressure across the Tennessee valley tracked up into the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes region, bringing a cold front through central North Carolina. A broken line of showers and storms tracked across the northern and northwest Piedmont and produced several reported downed trees across portions of the Triad and southern Piedmont. Storms exited the region by late evening.
episodes.189786: A strong upper level trough over the southern Appalachians pivoted across the Carolinas during the evening. This resulted in a band of showers and embedded storms across portions of central North Carolina. Numerous downed trees were reported as a result of strong downdrafts across the southern Piedmont, Sandhills, and southern Coastal Plain.
episodes.190071: An advancing low pressure system entered into the Ohio Valley on April 11th and set forth strong thunderstorms and heavy downpours. Storms tracked through initially early in the afternoon, stirring up strong winds that blew down a tree near the town of Ironton. As multiple rounds of showers and storms pressed across Ohio, heavy downpours over already saturated soils drained into the local creeks and streams and resulted in river flooding beginning that evening. Flooding eventually stemmed into the Ohio River on the 13th as water flowed down from New York and Pennsylvania, where heavy rain also occurred. Several gauges along the Ohio River from Willow Island Lock, Marietta, and Pomeroy rose above flood stage, resulting in flooded streets in the nearby towns. The river returned below flood at all three locations on April 14th and 15th.
episodes.190398: A major flash flood event occurred across portions of the Florida big bend and southern Georgia during the late night hours of April 10th through the early morning hours of April 11th.  Between 6 and 10 inches of rain fell with localized higher amounts, particularly over Tallahassee.  This resulted in rapid water rises across Tallahassee with numerous cars and structures flooded.  Several million dollars in flood damage occurred.  The Godby High School campus was flooded in Tallahassee, resulting in at least $250K in damage just to that school.  Surrounding rural areas of the Florida big bend and southern Georgia also saw numerous flooded roadways. The Lowndes County, GA area including Valdosta saw at least 70 locations with water covering roadways.  The primary cause of the event was a slow moving line of thunderstorms that trained repeatedly over the same locations.
episodes.190435: A deep and moisture rich storm system tracked across western New York on the night of Thursday April 11th and into the morning on Friday April 12th. Periods of steady and at times heavy rain fell across portions of the area, especially western New York. A Flood Warning was issued on the morning of the 12th for a large portion of the Niagara Frontier and points south to the western Southern Tier for excessive rainfall that had the potential to cause flooding in low-lying areas, urban areas and for small streams. ||Flooding was reported in Clarence Center on Lapp Road, resulting in a portion of the road being closed.
episodes.190466: An area of low pressure tracked across the area during the evening hours. Numerous showers and thunderstorms were associated with this system. Some of these storms reached severe levels, producing damaging winds over mainly the northwest North Carolina Foothills region and one tornado in Wilkes County.
episodes.190477: An area of low pressure tracked across the area during the evening hours. Numerous showers and thunderstorms were associated with this system. Some of these storms reached severe levels, producing damaging winds over mainly portions of the Piedmont region of southwest Virginia and one tornado in Pittsylvania County.
episodes.190633: Showers and a few thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.190969: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms and small lines of storms developed across western North Carolina ahead of a cold front during the afternoon and evening. Multiple strong to severe storms developed, producing one tornado and several areas of damaging straight line winds.
episodes.191015: A frontal boundary became stationary across the heart of the Ark-La-Tex region in vicinity of the Interstate 30 corridor on April 8th before slowly advancing southeast on April 9th. Concurrently, very moist southwest flow aloft resulting from a nearly cut-off low across the Desert Southwest provided for precipitable water values near 2 inches.    Thunderstorms developed and gradually spread northward from Central into Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and Northern Louisiana in the afternoon and evening on April 8th and continued throughout April 9th before gradually tapering off early on the 10th, resulting in widespread rainfall amounts of 4-8 inches across the region. This convection also occurred along the northern periphery of deeper returning low-level moisture with MLCAPE in excess of 1500 J/kg and favorable deep-layer shear. As a result, the threat of large hail and gusty winds increased by late afternoon into the early evening on April 8th and early on April 9th. As the low-level jet strengthened, convection became more organized with a few supercells and increasing thunderstorm clusters. During this timeframe, numerous reports damaging wind gusts and flash flooding were received across Northern Louisiana.
episodes.191023: A strengthening low pressure system and several frontal boundaries all came together across eastern Kentucky during the day on April 11, 2024. Radar showed scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across the state through much of the day. By the early afternoon, SPC issued a watch for the far eastern portion of the state and into neighboring western Virginia, much of West Virginia, and Southeast Ohio. The main concern was fast moving storms and the potential for a few supercells, which could result in strong wind gusts to 70mph and a few tornadoes. Indeed, things did ramp up across portions of eastern KY, specifically in Pike and Magoffin counties. Thankfully there were no tornadoes reported, and the damage was fairly minimal, limited to trees down along the roadways. Meanwhile, a flood prone area in Floyd County also received enough rain to cause issues by the evening.
episodes.191026: Heavy rain brought flooding to the Ouachita River during the middle of April 2024.
episodes.191063: After the low pressure system and multiple fronts passed through on the 11th, having caused damage to far eastern Kentucky, the system moved to the northeast, where it combined into one very strong surface low pressure system by April 12th. This system then generated a secondary boundary which moved around the west side of the low and back into Kentucky during the day of the 12th. More scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon as a result along this boundary. One storm in Whitley County resulted in severe winds which damaged trees in the Gausdale community.

The Shade River near Chester rose above its bankfull level on the morning of April 12th. After cresting around 17.9 feet that evening, waters receded below bankfull early the next morning. A few low lying spots along Scout Camp Road near the Sugar Run Creek bridge flooded as a result of the river spilling out of its banks.
A portion of Lapp Road in Clarence Center was closed due to flooding.

Widespread heavy rainfall of six to ten inches occurred across much of the Sabine River basin of East Texas and West Central Louisiana Parish April 8th through April 10th, inundating the basin and especially points farther downstream and namely at Logansport. As a result, the Sabine River rose rapidly into moderate flood stage (32 feet) early on April 12th and eventually crested near 33.4 feet on April 13th. The river remained in moderate flood stage through late afternoon on April 15th before receding through the latter half of April.

At Glenville, the Little Kanawha River rose above its 23 foot flood stage on the morning of April 12th. The river crested to around 25 feet that afternoon and then receded below flood stage again the same evening. Flooding impacted most of Elm Street and sections of Brooklyn Drive and River Street during this time.
Flooding occurred along Route 60 from Hurricane to Teays Valley.

Winds generally gusted 45 to 55 mph. One of the strongest gusts was 58 mph at a mesonet site near Woods Hole at 11:01 AM EDT. There was also a 64 mph gust from a mesonet site at Conimicut Light in Rhode Island at 8:42 AM EDT.
Camp Virgil Tate Road flooded at the entrance to Camp Virgil Tate.

Emergency managers reported flash flooding along with multiple evacuations in the Wailua area. Additionally a large crane at the Wailua River was leaning on a power line and blocking a road. Several roads were impassable due to flooding. Wailua Bridge southbound lane was closed due to flash flooding.

Multiple Roads in Koloa were impassable and closed due to flooding which was caused by the heavy rainfall. A small landslide was reported near Piko Road. Additionally, Poipu Road and Koloa Road were flooded and water entered storefront properties. There were several evacuations in the area.
Flooding was reported for 100 yards in the vicinity of Kaumakani/Pakala area.
Olohena Road was closed near the solar farm due to flooding and a landslide.
Halehaka Road was closed due to a downed tree.
Hulemalu Road near Alekoko Menehune Fishpond was closed due to fallen trees and boulders.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused RT 5 near the intersection of Shepherds River Rd. to be reduced to one lane due to flooding.
Flooding observed on State Route 18 about three quarters of a mile before Crystal Lake.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused Bond Spring Road in Newfield near the intersection of Shady Nook Road flooded in one lane.
Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt caused Route 17 to flood and cut off a main thruway to Rangeley. The flooding was the result of overland water and not from a river.
Flooding from the Pocatalico River impacted Cicerone Road in Walton.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused excessive runoff of Rand Mountain and flash flooding along Bachelor Brook in Weld. The rapid rise caused a 30 foot washout to one lane of Byron Road.
Heavy rain caused standing water along Route 173 near Trues Pond Road.
Rain and snowmelt caused the Lincoln Brook to flood washing out a 20-foot section Lincoln Pond Road in Rangeley.

Heavy rain and snowmelt caused the Swift River to rise and flood portions of Route 17 near Houghton Road in Byron. The USGS river gage on the Swift River at Roxbury crested at 9.1 feet around 3 PM, exceeding the 7 foot flood stage.
Heavy rain cause excessive runoff along high terrain near Stickney Corner, flooding one lane of Route 220.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused Rapid Stream Road in Kingfield to washout from the Rapid Stream overflowing it's banks.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused minor washout on Plaisted Road in Jay.
Flooding was reported along New York Route 5 between Mckinley Road near Palatine Bridge and Reservoir Road.
Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt caused Stratton Brook Pond Road in Stratton to washout from Stratton Brook overflowing its banks and flooding the road.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused Route 27 in Eustis was closed in multiple spots between Beaudry Road and Bartlett Road due to flooding along the North Branch of the Dead River.

Little Tygart Creek at Mineral Wells climbed above its 11 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of April 12th, then continued to rise to a crest of around 15.3 feet the following evening. Backwater from of the Ohio River sustained flooding along Little Tygart Creek until the morning of the 15th. This level of flooding impacted most of Speedway Road and sections of Woodridge Drive and Dickens Drive. Flooding also reached a home on Mayo Drive above the intersection with Irene Lane.
Heavy rain and snowmelt caused flooding along the Sandy River caused Main Street near Smalls Falls in Rangeley to close.
Photos were sent in by a trained spotter reporting trees downed or damaged in the Gausdale community as a thunderstorm moved through. The spotter noted that the wind arrived in one huge gust.
County dispatch reported Modoc Rd in Madison was washed out due to excessive rainfall and snowmelt.

Heavy Rain and snowmelt caused the Pemigewasset River to come out of its banks and flood parts of Plymouth and Holderness. The flooding began on the early evening of the 12th and continued for about 24 hours, cresting in the early morning hours of the 13th. The flood stage at the USGS river gage in Plymouth is 13 feet, and the river crested around 16.1 feet. The most impacted area was flooding of Route 175A and portions of PSU recreational facilities.
Trees and powerlines were reported down along south and north Randolph St, as well as north Lee St and Rockingham Rd in the town of Rockingham.
Multiple trees were blown down in the area of Safie 3rd St and Safie 4th St in east Rockingham.
A tree was blown down onto a residence along Hide Away Lane in Hamlet.

A tree was blown down onto powerlines along George Dawkins Drive north of North Carolina highway 177. Numerous other trees were reported down in Hamlet, including along Boyd Lake Rd, Palm St, and Charlotte St.
Trees were blown down along Old Wire Rd, Turnpike Rd and Aberdeen Rd. Numerous other trees and powerlines were reported down across the county.
A tree was blown down near the 300 block of North Fulton St in Raeford.
The public reported trees uprooted and snapped near the intersection of Riverton Rd and Airbase Rd.
A tree was blown down near the 500 block of East Edinborough Ave in Raeford.
Trees were blown down near the intersection of Walter Gibson Rd and Blue Springs Rd in Antioch.
A tree was blown down on North Old Wire Rd.
A tree was blown down near the intersection of Arabia Rd and McGougan Rd.
Trees were reported down along Crystal Springs Rd.
The Fayetteville Regional Airport measured a gust of 59 mph.
Trees were reported down along Doc Bennett Rd near Fayetteville regional airport.
Multiple trees were reported down in the Autryville area, especially along Yellow Skin Rd.

The first and primary visible damage of the tornado occurred at a property just off North Knoweshaw Road, near the intersection of the AA Highway. Here, notable damage occurred to an outbuilding, with a complete collapse of the wall structures. There were several trees that were broken and uprooted on this property as well, but the damage to the outbuilding was just enough to classify this tornado as an EF-1, with wind speeds estimated around 90 mph. ||Video footage was captured of this tornado crossing the AA Highway. The only other damage that occurred was at a property just on the south side of the AA Highway after the tornado crossed it. The primary damage here was hardwood trees that were broken.  One of the windows was broken at the dwelling on this property as well. After this property, no other damage was reported, but there was insulation and other debris that was thrown across the fields southeast of this property, with the last known debris found at a nearby landfill. No property damage was observed at the landfill.
Reports of multiple large trees and power lines down.

The Ohio River at Parkersburg rose above flood stage just after midnight on the 13th of April. The river reached a crest of around 38.5 feet early the next morning, then fell below flood stage before sunrise on the 15th. Several homes flooded in the Happy Valley and Point Drive areas near Parkersburg, along the Little Kanawha River. A few homes flooded on Annas Drive in Vienna, West Virginia, as well as Dave's Marina, Walnut Street, and Scott Avenue in Belpre, Ohio.

The Ohio River at Belleville Lock rose above its 35 foot flood stage on the evening of April 12th and then continued to rise to a crest of around 40.1 feet on the morning of the 14th. The river eventually receded below flood stage again the afternoon of April 15. While spilled out of its banks, Route 124 and sections of Ohio State Route 248 at Sand Hill were flooded.
Multiple trees were reported down in the Salemburg area, especially along Salemburg highway.
One half dozen trees down and powerlines as well.

Leon County Emergency Management reported road closures along Capitola Road between Chaires Crossroad and Baum Road due to water covering roadways. This flooding was slow to recede and persisted for several days after the heavy rain ended.
Large tree down.
Measured gust in Elizabethtown.
A few trees were reported down in the Turkey area between Turkey Highway and Old Warsaw Rd.
Large tree down and NC 41 was closed.
Trees were reported down across the county. The time was estimated based on radar.
Powerlines were damaged in and around Warsaw.
